title: Cancer Trial Drug Zavondemstat Works Through Unexpected Target, Study Finds
excerpt: A study in Nature Chemical Biology finds the drug acts mainly by blocking the DNA-building enzyme DHODH, not the KDM4 proteins it was designed to hit — with implications for patient selection in trials.
body:
• The experimental cancer drug zavondemstat, currently being tested in patients, does not primarily act on the KDM4 proteins it was designed to block, researchers report in the journal Nature Chemical Biology.
  • Experiments in patient-derived glioblastoma stem cells traced most of the drug's anti-cancer effect to DHODH, an enzyme that supplies the molecular building blocks for new DNA.
  • The misidentified mechanism could have skewed patient selection in clinical trials and cast doubt on years of published research that used the related compound QC6352 to study KDM4 biology.
  • The study does not show that zavondemstat is ineffective against cancer — it shows the drug kills cancer cells through a different route than assumed, which changes how trials should select patients.

An experimental cancer drug currently being tested in patients may have entered clinical trials on the basis of a fundamentally mistaken understanding of how it works, according to a study published October 6 in Nature Chemical Biology. The research, led by the University of Sydney in collaboration with Goethe University, the University of Oxford and the Institute of Cancer Research in London, reports that the drug zavondemstat — developed to treat cancers including colorectal, pancreatic and prostate cancer — derives most of its anti-cancer activity not from its designed target but from blocking a different enzyme entirely.

The discovery emerged while her team was testing whether zavondemstat and a related research compound, QC6352, could be repurposed for glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive brain cancer. Using patient-derived glioblastoma stem cells, tumor models and genetic, mechanistic and molecular experiments, the researchers traced the compounds' effects to DHODH — an enzyme cancer cells rely on to manufacture the nucleotides needed for rapid DNA copying — rather than the intended KDM4 target.

Context & Background

Zavondemstat was developed as an inhibitor of KDM4, a family of proteins that function as epigenetic regulators, modifying histones — the protein scaffolds around which DNA is wound — to influence which genes are switched on. When overactive, KDM4 proteins can drive the growth and spread of cancer cells, and their overactivity has been linked to several aggressive tumor types. The drug entered clinical testing on the assumption that blocking KDM4 was the key to its therapeutic effect.

https://x.com/medical_xpress/status/2107494565900927113

The first clue that something was off came from a control experiment. When the researchers tested other KDM4 inhibitors alongside QC6352 in glioblastoma cells, the others failed to reproduce QC6352's anti-cancer effects. If blocking KDM4 were truly driving the activity, other inhibitors of the same target should have behaved similarly — the divergence pointed to QC6352 acting through a different mechanism entirely.

That investigation converged on DHODH, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, an enzyme in the pyrimidine synthesis pathway. Munoz offered a vivid analogy: DHODH is a machine producing the bricks needed to build new DNA. Switch off the machine, and the cell runs out of bricks — it can no longer copy its DNA or keep dividing. In short, the compounds are not reprogramming the epigenetic state of cancer cells; they are starving them of the nucleotides needed for DNA synthesis, a fundamentally different form of metabolic stress.

Impact & Analysis

The practical concern is clinical. Trials of targeted cancer therapies typically enroll patients whose tumors show evidence of the presumed target, on the logic that those patients are most likely to benefit. If zavondemstat's true target is DHODH rather than KDM4, the biomarker strategy may select patients unlikely to respond while excluding patients who could benefit from DHODH inhibition.

"Getting a drug's mechanism wrong can lead to poorly designed clinical trials, inappropriate patient selection and years of research focused on the wrong biological target."

— Professor Lenka Munoz, University of Sydney

The research-tool fallout may be even broader. QC6352 has been used around the world as a leading tool compound to study KDM4 biology, so a substantial body of published research may have drawn conclusions about KDM4 function from experiments in which the compound was, in fact, hitting a different target. Misattributed mechanisms can propagate through the literature, shaping hypotheses, grant funding and drug-discovery programs in ways that are difficult to unwind.

There is also a therapeutic upside. DHODH inhibition has attracted growing interest in oncology, and several drugs targeting the enzyme are already being investigated for other cancers. The findings point to DHODH inhibition as a potential new avenue for glioblastoma, one of the deadliest human cancers, and any mechanism-based strategy that can be pursued with compounds already in clinical development offers a faster route to the clinic than starting from scratch. Separately, the researchers developed new compounds that inhibit KDM4 without affecting DHODH, giving scientists cleaner chemical probes to study the genuine role of KDM4 in cancer.

Diaspora Angle

For readers following cancer research, the episode underscores why precision oncology trials increasingly hinge on biomarker accuracy: being enrolled in a trial is only as useful as the match between the drug and the biology it is assumed to target, a standard that applies to patients wherever trials run.

What's Next

Zavondemstat continues its journey through clinical development, and the authors are not calling for it to be halted — they are calling for its development to be re-anchored to the correct mechanism, with patient-selection criteria to match. Watch for whether the ongoing trials publish revised biomarker strategies, and whether DHODH-targeting compounds already in development for other cancers are proposed for testing in brain-cancer patients.
